land.text: Portuguese Guinea: independence was 'unilaterally declared on 24 September 1973' and Portugal 'granted full independence ... on September 10, 1974'

predecessors.note: Portugal's colony was part of the Estado Novo shape; no separate Portuguese Guinea row exists in Cliopatria (a counterpart dossier is listed in the report).

capitals.name: Bissau
capitals.note: Infobox 'Bissau 11°52′N 15°36′W'. Until September 1974 the city was held by Portugal; the page says the People's National Assembly declared independence at Madina do Boé on 23-24 September 1973 (War of Independence page).

keyframe_review.note: 32,871 km2 for 1973-2023 against the infobox 'covers 36,125 square kilometres' (ratio 0.91, no year). The shape is the whole country from September 1973, although the PAIGC then held 'most of the country' and Portuguese forces 'were largely confined to the major cities and a diminished collection of fortified camps' until the Algiers accord of 1974: a contest event carries 1973-1974.
Same outline as 1973-2023 (32,871 km2); no border change is recorded on the page.

region.text: the PAIGC's liberated zones, 'most of the country' in 1972-1973, within the colony of Portuguese Guinea

ledger.note: 24 September 1973: the PAIGC's People's National Assembly declares the independence of the Republic of Guinea-Bissau. 'On 23-24 September 1973, the People's National Assembly ... met in Madina do Boé ... and declared the independence of the Republic of Guinea-Bissau'; 'before the end of the year, the new Republic of Guinea-Bissau had been recognised by at least 57 states', and on 2 November 1973 the UN General Assembly voted 93 to 7 on a resolution in its favour. The Guinea-Bissau page: 'Independence was unilaterally declared on 24 September 1973.'

region.text: the whole country: PAIGC liberated zones, with Portuguese forces confined to the major cities and camps

ledger.note: September 1973: Portuguese forces still hold the cities. 'By then, Portuguese forces were largely confined to the major cities and a diminished collection of fortified camps'; 'By the beginning of 1972, although territorial boundaries remained blurry, most of the country belonged to one of PAIGC's liberated zones.' The page gives no list of towns, so the contested zone is drawn as the whole country.

region.text: the whole country, the cities and camps passing from Portuguese forces to Guinea-Bissau

ledger.note: 10 September 1974: Portugal grants full independence. 'On 26 August 1974, in Algiers, Portugal and the PAIGC signed an accord in which Portugal agreed to recognise Guinea-Bissau's independence and to remove all troops by the end of October'; 'As stipulated in the Algiers accord, Portugal granted full independence to Guinea-Bissau on September 10, 1974'. The Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 overthrew the regime in Lisbon; the infobox dates the war 'January 23, 1963 - September 10, 1974'.

wars.name: Guinea-Bissau War of Independence

zones.text: the whole country: PAIGC liberated zones against Portuguese-held cities and camps

wars.outcome: Algiers Accord (infobox 'Result'): Portugal recognised Guinea-Bissau's independence and withdrew; full independence granted on 10 September 1974.
wars.note: The page says the PAIGC 'effectively controlled 2/3 of Portuguese Guinea' by 1967 and 'most of the country' by early 1972; Amilcar Cabral was assassinated in Conakry on 20 January 1973; Portugal attacked the PAIGC-held island of Como in April 1964 and launched Operation Green Sea against Guinea-Conakry in late November 1970. The war began on 23 January 1963 (infobox 'January 23, 1963 - September 10, 1974'), ten years before the state; the entry starts with the state in 1973 (review af-08-l) and only 1973-1974 is in the ledger.

wars.name: Guinea-Bissau Civil War
wars.outcome: 'An army uprising in May 1998 led to the Guinea-Bissau Civil War and the president's ousting in June 1999.' No territorial change is recorded.
wars.note: The page gives no zone of fighting.

certainty.note: The PAIGC's liberated zones had blurry edges ('territorial boundaries remained blurry'); the cities were Portuguese.

Judgement, not read in the pages opened: the frontiers with Senegal and Guinea are colonial treaty lines; the Guinea-Bissau page records no border dispute and says only that the Casamance region 'was ceded' to the French in 1886.

notes: Two pages (budget 1-2). NOT SETTLED: (1) Cliopatria's shape begins 1973 and covers the whole country, but until 10 September 1974 Portugal held the cities and camps; the dossier draws 1973-09 to 1974-09 as a contest with estado-novo over the whole country, which is coarse (the PAIGC held 'most of the country', no percentage for 1973) and a gap-filler could replace it with an occupation of the named Portuguese-held towns if a page lists them. (2) Portuguese Guinea has no Cliopatria row and no dossier; the Estado Novo shape (1967-1975) contains the territory, so estado-novo is used as counterpart; a dossier for the PAIGC's liberated zones or for Portuguese Guinea 1879-1974 (the Portuguese Guinea group) would give the other side of these events. (3) The union with Cape Verde and its end after the 14 November 1980 coup of Joao Bernardo Vieira (page: 'On 14 November 1980, Joao Bernardo Vieira' overthrew President Luis Cabral; the anthem was 'shared with Cape Verde' until 1996) is not described as a union on the Guinea-Bissau page; no event is written. (4) The Madina do Boé site is not in the gazetteer and the capital entry is Bissau throughout. (5) The 2012 and 2025 coups are dated on the page but move no border. (6) The infobox area exceeds Cliopatria's by 10 percent; the page does not say whether it includes the Bijagos islands, which may lie inside Cliopatria's bbox (-16.66 to -13.58, 10.96 to 12.63). No ruler strip: the pages opened give no list.
